text.S1: The wife of a rich man fell sick, and as she felt that her end was drawing near, she called her only daughter to her bedside and said, "Dear child, be good and pious, and then the good God will always protect thee, and I will look down on thee from heaven and be near thee." Thereupon she closed her eyes and departed.
text.S2: The wife of a rich man fell sick, and when she felt that her death was near, she called her only daughter to her bedside and said, "My beloved child, be good and pious, and then God will always protect thee, and I will look down on thee from heaven and be near thee." After saying so she closed her eyes and died.
text.T1: Mkazi wa munthu wolemera anadwala,ndipo pamene anamvera kuti ali pafupi kufa, anayitana mwana wake yekha wamkazi pafupindi bedi ali cigonere nati, “Mwana wanga wokondedwa, uyenera kukhala munthu wabwino ndi wodzipereka kwa Mulungu, ndipo Iyeyo adzakuteteza nthawi zonse, ndipo ine ndidzakuyang’anira kucokera kumwamba ndi kukhala pafupi nawe.” Atatero, amayi ake anatseka maso awo ndi kufa.
text.T2: Mkazi wa munthu wolemera anadwala, ndipo pamene anamvera kuti ali pafupi kufa, anayitana mwana wake yekha wamkazi pafupi ndi bedi ali cigonere nati, “Mwana wanga wokondedwa, uyenera kukhala munthu wabwino ndi wodzipereka pa zauzimu, ndipo Mulungu adzakuteteza nthawi zonse, ndiponso ine ndidzakuyang’anira kucokera kumwamba ndi kukhala pafupi nawe.” Atatero, amayi ake anatseka maso awo ndi kumwalira.

text.S1: When winter came the snow spread a white sheet over the grave, and when the spring sun had drawn it off again, the man had taken another wife. The woman had brought two daughters into the house with her, who were beautiful and fair of face, but vile and black of heart. Now began a bad time for the poor step-child. They took her pretty clothes away from her, put an old gray bedgown on her, and gave her wooden shoes. "Just look at the proud princess, how decked out she is!" they cried, and laughed, and led her into the kitchen.
text.S2: When winter came, the snow spread over the grave, and when the spring sun melted it off again, the man married another woman. The woman had brought two daughters into the house with her, who were beautiful and fair of face, but they were very had hearted. Now began a bad time for the poor step-child. They took her pretty clothes away from her, put an old gray bed gown on her, and gave her wooden shoes. "Just look at the king’s daughter, how decked out she is!" they cried, and laughed, and took her into the kitchen.
text.T1: Nyengo yozizira itafika, cipale cofewa cinamwazikira pa manda, ndipo pamene dzuwa la m’chisanu linasungunula cipale cofewaco, m’zibambo anali atakwatira mkazi wina. Mzimayi anabweretsa ana ake atsikana awiri m’nyumba, amene anali wokongola ndi nkhope zawo zowoneka bwino, koma iwowa anali woyipa mtima kwambiri. Tsopano nthawi yamasautso inayamba kwa mwana uja wopeza. Iwo anam’landa zovala zake zonse zabwino, ndi kumuveka malaya akale wombuwa, ogona nawo, ndi kum’patsa nsapato zopangidwa ndi matabwa. “Tapenyani mwana wamkazi wa mfumu, mmene amukometsera mmene akuwonekera!’’ iwo anakweza mawu awo kumunyodola, ndi kum’seka, ndi kum’pereka kucipinda cophikira.

text.S1: There she had to do hard work from morning till night, get up before daybreak, carry water, light fires, cook and wash. Besides this, the sisters did her every imaginable injury— they mocked her and emptied her peas and lentils into the ashes, so that she was forced to sit and pick them out again. In the evening when she had worked till she was weary she had no bed to go to, but had to sleep by the fireside in the ashes. And as on that account she always looked dusty and dirty, they called her Cinderella.
text.S2: There she did hard work from morning till night, get up before daybreak, carry water, light fires, cook and wash clothes. Besides this, the girls did her every imaginable injury— they mocked her and threw her peas and lentils into the ashes, so that she was forced to sit and pick them out again. In the evening after she had done hard work, she had no bed sleep on, but had to sleep by the fireside in the ashes. Because of what happened, she looked dirty and grey and they called her Cinderella.
text.T1: Kumeneko, iye amagwira nchito yolimba kucokera m’mawa mpakana usiku, amawuka m’mamawa, kukatunga madzi, kuyatsa moto, kuphika ndi kuchapa zovala. Kuwonjezera pamenepa, atsikana aja anamucitira cinthu ciliconse copweteka– anam’seka ndipo anam’tayiranyemba zake ndi mbewu zina mphulusa, kotero kuti anaumirizidwa kukhala pansi ndi kuzitolanso nyemba zija. M’madzulo, pambuyopogwira nchito yotopetsa analibe pogona, koma amangogona m’mphepete mwa moto, m’phulusa. Cifukwa ca cocitika ici, iye amawoneka wombuwa ndi wadothi, ndipo iwo anamucha kuti Cinderella.
text.T2: Kumeneko, iye amagwira nchito yolimba kucokera m’mawa mpakana usiku, amawuka m’mamawa, kukatunga madzi, kuyatsa moto, kuphika ndi kuchapa zovala. text.S1: It happened that the father was once going to the fair, and he asked his two step-daughters what he should bring back for them. "Beautiful dresses," said one, "Pearls and jewels," said the second. "And thou, Cinderella," said he, "what wilt thou have?" "Father, break off for me the first branch which knocks against your hat on your way home."
text.S2: One time, it happened that the father was once going to the fair, and he asked his two step-daughters what he should bring back for them. "Beautiful dresses," said one, "adornments," said the second. "And thou, Cinderella," said he, "what wilt thou have?" "Father, pick for me the first branch which knocks against your hat on your way home."
text.T1: Nthawi ina, zinacitika kuti atate awo amapita kuciwonetsero, ndipo anapempha ana awo awiri aja opeza kuti n’ciyani comwe angawabweretsere. “Madelesi abwino,’’anatero m’modzi mwaiwo, “Ngale ndi zokongoletsera zamtengo wapatali,” anatero waciwiri. “Ndipo nanga, Cinderella,’’ iwo anatero, “kodi iwe udzafuna ciyani?’’ “Atate,munditholere nthambi yoyamba imene imagunda pa cipewa canu pobwerera kuno kunyumba.”
text.T2: Nthawi ina, zinacitika kuti atate awo amapita kuciwonetsero, ndipo anafunsa ana awo awiri aja opeza kuti n’ciyani comwe angawabweretsere. “Madelesi abwino,’’anatero m’modzi mwaiwo, “Ngale ndi zokongoletsera zamtengo wapatali,” anatero waciwiri. “Ndipo iweyo, Cinderella,’’ iwo anatero, “kodi iwe udzafuna ciyani?’’ “Atate,mundithyolere nthambi yoyamba imene idzagunda pa cipewa canu pobwerera kuno kunyumba.”

text.S1: So he bought beautiful dresses, pearls and jewels for his two step-daughters, and on his way home, as he was riding through a green thicket, a hazel twig brushed against him and knocked off his hat. Then he broke off the branch and took it with him. When he reached home he gave his step-daughters the things which they had wished for, and to Cinderella he gave the branch from the hazel-bush. Cinderella thanked him, went to her mother's grave and planted the branch on it, and wept so much that the tears fell down on it and watered it.
text.S2: So he bought beautiful dresses, pearls and jewels for his two step-daughters, and on his way home, as he went through a green thicket, a hazel twig brushed against him and knocked off his hat. Then he broke off the branch and took it with him. When he reached home he gave his step-daughters the things they had wished for, and to Cinderella he gave the small branch from a tree. Cinderella thanked him and went with it to her mother's grave and planted the branch on it, and wept so much that the tears fell down on it and watered the branch.
text.T1: Conco iwo anagula madelesi wokongola, ngale ndi zokongoletsera zamtengo wapatali za ana awo aja opeza, ndipo pomwe amabwerera kunyumba, anakwera pa bulu mnkhalango yamsipu, nthambi yaing’ono inawakhudza ndikugwetsa cipewa cawo. Pambuyo pake, iwo anathyolako nthambiyo ndi kupita nayo kunyumba. Atafika kunyumba, anapatsa ana awo opeza aja zomwe anamafuna, ndipo kwa Cinderella, iwo anam’patsa nthambi yaing’ono ya mtengo. Cinderella anawayamikira atate ake, ndipo anapita nayo kumanda kwa amayi ake ndi kuyibzala nthambiyo pamandapo, ndipo analira kwambiri kotero kuti misozi inagwerapo ndikuyithirira nthambi ija.
text.T2: Conco iwo anagula madelesi wokongola, ngale ndi zovala za miyala yamtengo wapatali za ana awo aja opeza, ndipo pomwe amabwerera kunyumba, anapitira mnkhalango yamsipu, nthambi yaing’ono ya mtengo wa hazel inawakhudza ndikugwetsa cipewa cawo. Cinderella anawayamikira atate ake, ndipo anapita nayo kumanda kwa amayi ake ndi kuyibzala nthambiyo pamandapo, ndipo analira kwambiri kotero kuti misozi inagwerapo ndikuyithirira nthambi ija.

text.S1: And it grew, however, and became a handsome tree. Twice a day Cinderella went and sat beneath it, and wept and prayed, and a little white bird always came on the tree, and if Cinderella expressed a wish, the bird would throw down to her what she had wished for.

text.T1: Nthambi ija ya Mtengo inakula,ndipo indakhala mtengo wokongola.Kawiri patsiku Cinderella amapita kukakhala m’munsi mwamtengowo, nalira komanso ndi kupemphera, ndipo kambalame kakang’ono koyera kamabwera nthawi zonse pamtengowo,ndipo ngati Cinderella amafuna cinthu ciliconse, mbalameyo imaponya cinthuco cimene iye anafuna.

text.S1: It happened, however, that the King appointed a festival which was to last three days, and to which all the beautiful young girls in the country were invited. When the two stepsisters heard that they too were to appear among the number, they were delighted, called Cinderella and said, "Comb our hair for us, brush our shoes and fasten our buckles, for we are going to the festival at the King's palace." Cinderella obeyed, but wept because she too would have liked to go to the dance, and begged her step-mother to allow her to do so.
text.S2: It happened that the King appointed a festival which was to last three days, and to which all the beautiful young girls in the country were invited. When the two stepsisters heard that they too will be at the festival, they were delighted, called Cinderella and said, "Comb our hair for us, brush our shoes and fasten our buckles, for we are going to the festival at the King's palace." Cinderella obeyed, but wept because she too would have liked to go to the dance, and begged her step-mother to allow her to go with them.
text.T1: Zinacitika kuti Mfumu ya ndodo inapanga tsiku lacikondwererero cimene cinadzachitika masiku atatu, ndipo kumene atsikana okongola acicepere m’dzikolo anali atayitanidwa. Pamene atsikana awiri aja opeza anamva kuti nawonso adzakhalako kucindwerereco, anakondwera kwambiri, anayitana Cinderella ndipo anati “Pesa tsitsi lathu, pukuta nsapato zathu ndipo manga malamba athu cifukwa tikupita kucikondwererero ca kunyumba Yamfumu yandodo.’’ Cinderella anavemera ndi kucita, koma analira cifukwa nayenso anafunitsitsa kuti angakapezekeko, akanakonda kupita kukavina, ndipo anapempha amayi ake wopeza kuti amulole kupita nawo.

text.S1: "Thou go, Cinderella!" said she; "Thou art dusty and dirty and wouldst go to the festival? Thou hast no clothes and shoes, and yet wouldst dance!" As, however, Cinderella went on asking, the step-mother at last said, "I have emptied a dish of lentils into the ashes for thee, if thou hast picked them out again in two hours, thou shalt go with us." The maiden went through the back-door into the garden, and called, "You tame pigeons, you turtle-doves, and all you birds beneath the sky, come and help me to pick the good into the pot, the bad into the crop."
text.S2: "Thou go, Cinderella!" said she; "You are dusty and dirty and would you go to the festival? You don’t have clothes and shoes, and yet you want to dance!" Even so, Cinderella went on asking, the step-mother at last said, "I have emptied a dish of lentils into the ashes for thee, if you picked them within two hours, you will go with us." The girl went through the back-door into the garden, and asked for help, "You tame pigeons, you turtle-doves, and all you birds under the sky, come and help me to pick the good into the pot, the bad into the crop."
text.T1: “Nawenso ungapite,Cinderella’’ anatero amayi ake; “Ndiwe wombuwa ndi wadothi ndipo ukufunabe kupita kucikondwererero? Ndipo ngakhale kuti ulibe zovala ndi nsapato, koma ufuna upita kugule!’’ Komabe, Cinderella anapitiriza kupempha, ndipo amayi ake wopeza potsirizira anati, “Ndakhutula mbewu mpimo wa dishi m’phulusa kuti iweyouzitole pambuyo pa m’maola awiri, ndipoungapite nafe pamodzi,’’ Mtsikana uja anapita kumbuyo kwa dimba, ndikupempha thandizo, “Inu njiwa, inu nkhunda, ndi inu mbalamezonse zili pansi pathambo, bwerani mundithandize kuyika katundu wabwino uyu m’poto, kucotsa zoipa m’mbewu izi.”
text.T2: “Mupita Cinderella!’’ anatero amayi ake; “Ndiwe wombuwa ndi wadothi ndipo ukufunabe kupita kucikondwererero? Ulibe zovala ndi nsapato, koma ufuna upita kugule!’’ Komabe, Cinderella anapitiriza kupempha, ndipo amayi ake wopeza potsirizira anati, “Ndakhutula mbale ya khobwe zako m’phulusa kuti iweyo uzitole pambuyo pa m’maola awiri, ndipo udzapita nafe pamodzi,’’ Mtsikana uja anapita kucitseko cakumbuyo kwa nyumba mpaka mdimba, ndikupempha thandizo, “Inu nkhunda, inu njiwa, ndi inu mbalame zonse zili pansi pathambo, bwerani mundithandize kuyika zabwino m’poto, zoipa m’mbewu.”

text.S1: Then two white pigeons came in by the kitchen-window, and afterwards the turtle-doves, and at last all the birds beneath the sky, came whirring and crowding in, and alighted amongst the ashes. And the pigeons nodded with their heads and began to pick, pick, pick, pick, and the rest also began to pick, pick, pick, pick, and gathered all the good grains into the dish. Hardly had one hour passed before they had finished, and all flew out again. Then the girl took the dish to her step-mother, and was glad, and believed that now she would be allowed to go with them to the festival. But the step-mother said, "No, Cinderella, thou hast no clothes and thou canst not dance; thou wouldst only b laughed at."

Nkhunda zinavomera pogwedeza mitu yawo ca m’mwamba ndi capansi kusonyeza kuvomera, ndipo zinayamba kutola, kutola, kutola, kutola ndipo mbalame zina zonse zinayamba kutola, kutola, kutola, kutola ndi kuziyika pamodzi mbewu zabwino m’mbale. Panali pasanapite ngakhale ola limodzi pomwe mbalame zija zinatsiriza nchito ija ndi kuwulukanso, kupita. Mtsikana uja ananyamula mbale kulipereka kwa amayi ake wopeza, anali wokondwa,akukhulupirira kuti iwo adzamulola kupita nawo kucikondwerero. Amayi ake wopeza anati, “Iyayi, Cinderella, ulibe zovala zabwino ndipo sungavine; adzangokuseka anthu iwe.’’

text.S1: They never once thought of Cinderella, and believed that she was sitting at home in the dirt, picking lentils out of the ashes. The prince went to meet her, took her by the hand and danced with her. He would dance with no other maiden, and never let loose of her hand, and if anyone else came to invite her, he said, "This is my partner.” She danced till it was evening, and then she wanted to go home. But the King's son said, "I will go with thee and bear thee company," for he wished to see to whom the beautiful maiden belonged. She escaped from him, however, and sprang into the pigeon-house. The King's son waited until her father came, and then he told him that the stranger maiden had leapt into the pigeon-house.

Sanavine ndi mtsikana winansoayi, ndipo sanafune kumutayirira, ndipo ngati wina afuna kubvina naye amati, ‘’Uyu ndiye mzanga.’’ Anabvina mpaka m’madzulo, ndipo anafuna kupita kunyumba. Koma mwana wa mfumu anati, “Ndidzapita nawe ndipo ndiwe mzanga,’’ anafuna kuwona kuti kodi ndi mwana wandani kumene kucokera mtsikanayu.Iye anamuzemba, ndi kuthamangira ku khola la nkhunda. Mwana wa mfumu anayembekezera mpaka atate ake anabwera, ndipo anawauza kuti mtsikana wacilendo wathawira kukhola la nkhunda.

text.S1: The old man thought, "Can it be Cinderella?" and they had to bring him an axe and a pickaxe that he might hew the pigeon-house to pieces, but no one was inside it. And when they got home Cinderella lay in her dirty clothes among the ashes, and a dim little oil-lamp was burning on the mantle-piece, for Cinderella had jumped quickly down from the back of the pigeon-house and had run to the little hazel-tree, and there she had taken off her beautiful clothes and laid them on the grave, and the bird had taken them away again, and then she had placed herself in the kitchen amongst the ashes in her gray gown.

text.S1: Next day when the festival began afresh, and her parents and the step- sisters had gone once more, Cinderella went to the hazel-tree and said—"Shiver and quiver, my little tree, Silver and gold throw down over me." Then the bird threw down a much more beautiful dress than on the preceding day. And when Cinderella appeared at the festival in this dress, everyone was astonished at her beauty. The King's son had waited until she came, and instantly took her by the hand and danced with no one but her. When others came and invited her, he said, "She is my partner." When evening came she wished to leave, and the King's son followed her and wanted to see which house she went to. But she sprang away from him, and into the garden behind the house.

text.S1: Therein stood a beautiful tall tree on which hung the most magnificent pears. She clambered so nimbly between the branches like a squirrel that the King's son did not know where she was gone. He waited until her father came, and said to him, "The stranger-maiden has escaped from me, and I believe she has climbed up the pear-tree." The father thought, "Can it be Cinderella?" and had an axe brought and cut the tree down, but no one was on it. And when they got into the kitchen, Cinderella lay there amongst the ashes, as usual, for she had jumped down on the other side of the tree, had taken the beautiful dress to the bird on the little hazel-tree, and put on her gray gown.

text.S1: When evening came, Cinderella wished to leave, and the King's son was anxious to go with her, but she escaped from him so quickly that he could not follow her. The King's son had, however, used a stratagem, and had caused the whole staircase to be smeared with pitch, and there, when she ran down, had the maiden's left slipper remained sticking. The King's son picked it up, and it was small and dainty, and all golden. Next morning, he went with it to the fa- ther, and said to him, "No one shall be my wife but she whose foot this golden slipper fits."

text.S1: She first washed herhands and face clean, and then went and bowed down before the King's son, who gave her the golden shoe. Then she seated herself on a stool, drew her foot out of the heavy wooden shoe, and put it into the slipper, which fitted like a glove. And when she rose up and the King's son looked at her face he recognized the beautiful maiden who had danced with him and cried, "That is the true bride!" The step-mother and the two sisters were terrified and became pale with rage; he, however, took Cinderella on his horse and rode away with her. As they passed by the hazel-tree, the two white doves cried— "Turn and peep, turn and peep, The shoe is not too small," and when they had cried, the two came flying down and placed themselves on Cinderella's shoulders, one on the right, the other on the left, and remained sitting there.

text.T1: Poyamba anasamba m’manja ndi kumaso kwake, ndipo anapita nagwada pamaso pake pa mwana wa Mfumu, amene anamupatsa nsapato yake yagolide. Pambuyo pake anakhala pampando, anavula nsapato zopangidwa ndimatabwa, ndipo anabvala mapatapata ndipo zinakwanira bwino.Ndipo pamene anayimirira ndipo mwana wa Mfumu anamupenya nkhope, anazindikira nkhope ya namwali amene anavina naye ndipo anakweza mawu naati, “Zoona ndiye mkwatibwi!’’ Amayi ake wopeza ndi akulu ake anacita mantha kwambiri ndipo anagwetsa nkhope zawo ndi ukali; mkwati, anakwezeka Cinderella pa hosi yake napita naye. Pamene amadutsa mtengo umene uli pamanda a amayi ake, njiwa ziwiri zoyera zinakweza mawu niziti —‘’Tembenuka ndi kusuzumira, tembenuka ndi kusuzumira, Nsapato sizazing’ono,’’ ndipo zitalira, mbalalame ziwiri zinawuluka ndi kutera pamapewa a Cinderella, imodzi kudzanja lamanja, ndipo inayo kulamanzere, ndipo zinakhalabe pamenepo.

text.S1: When the wedding with the King's son had to be celebrated, the two false sisters came and wanted to get into favor with Cinderella and share her good fortune. When the betrothed couple went to church, the elder was at the right side and the younger at the left. Afterwards as they went back, the elder was at the left, and the younger at the right. And, for their wickedness and falsehood, they were punished with loneliness as long as they lived. And Cinderella lived happily ever after.

text.T1: Pamene cikondwerero caukwati wa mwana wa Mfumu cinacitika, akulu ake acinyengo anabwera ndipo amafuna kukonderakocokera kwa Cinderella ndi kuti agawane naye zabwino zimene anapeza. Pamene mkwati ndi mkwatibwi anapita kuchalichi, mkulu wake anali kudzanja lamanja,m’ng’ono wake kudzanja lamanzere. Pambuyo pake, pamene amabwerera, mkulu wake anali kulamanzere, ndipo m’ng’ono wake kudzanja lamanja. Ndipo, cifukwa coyipa mtima ndi cinyengo cawo, iwo analangidwa pokhala okha kwamoyo wawo wonse. Ndipo Cinderella anakhala pacikondwerero nthawi zonse.
